key: And thou shalt speak and say before the LORD thy God: ‘A wandering Aramean was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there, few in number; and he became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous.
s: The farmer bringing first fruits to the priest recites his people’s story; Rashi, on 26:5, reads the Aramean as Laban, who sought to uproot all in pursuing Jacob, his intent counted as the deed, and Ibn Ezra, on 26:5, as Jacob himself, poor and without means while in Aram.

evidence.gloss: [Rashi on 26:5, ‘an Aramean destroyed my father’, recalling the kindnesses of the Omnipresent:] Laban sought to uproot everything when he pursued Jacob, and because he intended to do it, the Omnipresent accounted it to him as though he had done it … [Ibn Ezra on 26:5, ‘oved avi’, after arguing that oved is intransitive:] and the likeliest is that the Aramean is Jacob, as if Scripture said: when my father was in Aram he was oved, and the sense is poor, without money.

reason: verse.js ok, ref Deuteronomy 26:5 and at [178,5] match (the straight opening quote of the recital made curly, as rule 8 allows). Plain sense faithful: 26:1 to 11 is the first-fruits rite, the basket set before the priest and a recital of the descent to Egypt, bondage and deliverance; no four-word run from the key. Read every packet source on 26:5 (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Rashbam, Sforno; Ramban and Deuteronomy Rabbah nothing). Rashi’s own words carry Laban seeking to uproot all when he pursued Jacob, his intent counted as the deed; Ibn Ezra’s own words carry the Aramean as Jacob, poor and without money while in Aram. A genuine difference (Ibn Ezra argues against the Laban reading), named without resolving (rule 5). The JPS rendering follows the wandering sense; the sentence attributes each reading to its commentator only. entry-check ok on scratch/V-d064-p.json.
